messages.subject: [statnet_help] Conditional ERGM?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet users,

I am working with a multiplex, two-mode network with two types of ties, A
and B.  In order for there to be a tie in B, then there must be a tie in A.

Suppose I want to run an ERGM for the ties in B only in cases where there
is a tie in A.  Is there a way for me to tell statnet to run the ERGM for B
only if A=1?  If so, I would love to see the command.

Any help would be most sincerely appreciated.

Michael

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Conditional ERGM?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Michael,

As it happens, the constraint atmost(nw), originally implemented for
fitting STERGMs should do exactly what you are asking.

BgivenA.fit <- ergm(B~model_terms, constraints=~atmost(A))

should fit a model conditional on B having no ties that are not in A.

This will work for the ergm 3.0-4 release (i.e., the one on CRAN), but I
would strongly recommend installing the preview release 3.0-999 (from
http://www.statnet.org/preview ), and using that, since it's likely to
be much, much faster at this particular problem. (You will also need to
install and load the add-on package tergm, since it's the one that
implements the atmost() constraint.)

                                        I hope this helps,
                                        Pavel

messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet Users,

I am estimating an ERGM on a bipartite network.  I have a number of node
covariates that apply to mode 1 but not to mode 2.  These are continuous
attributes, not categorical variables.  How do I include these covariates
in the ERGM?

Since these are continuous attributes, it seems that the b1factor and
b2factor terms are not appropriate.  However, because they apply only to a
subset of the nodes (i.e., mode 1), the nodecov command does not seem
appropriate either.

Any advice would be much appreciated.

Sincerely,

Michael

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Node Covariates in a Bipartite Network
messages.body_plain:
Dear Michael,

Indeed, this looks like a gap in our library of the statistics that we
should fill in.

In the meantime, you can use nodecov and set the vertex attribute such
that if it's a mode 1 covariate, its value for mode 2 nodes is 0, and
vice versa. This is mathematically equivalent to what a nodeb1cov and
nodeb2cov (if written) would do.

                          I hope this helps,
                          Pavel

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Upgrading ergm.userterms --- Please read if you use it.
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Upgrading ergm.userterms --- Please read if you use it.
messages.body_plain:
Dear ergm.userterms users,

The issue described in this note affects those who are currently using
ergm.userterms to implement their own ERGM terms. Those considering it
in the future (i.e., after the upcoming ergm 3.1 release) will not be
affected.

As you probably already know, ergm.userterms --- Statnet's mechanism
enabling users to write their own ERGM terms --- comes in a form of an R
package containing files for the user to put their own statistics into
(i.e., changestats.user.h, changestats.user.c, and InitErgmTerm.user.R),
as well as some boilerplate to support them (e.g., edgetree.h,
edgetree.c, changestat.h, changestat.c, etc.).

Although the ergm.userterms API is stable, recent developments in ergm
have necessitated the boilerplate files in ergm.userterms to be updated.
To reiterate, the user-written statistic source code
(changestats.user.h, changestats.user.c, and InitErgmTerm.user.R) can be
used without modification, but other files that came with the package
need to be changed.

To make things easier in the future, we have implemented a mechanism
(using R's LinkingTo API, in case you are wondering) that will keep
things in sync in releases after the upcoming one. However, for the
upcoming release, we need to transition to this new mechanism. For
someone using ergm.userterms, this transition entails the following
steps:
     1. Download the up-to-date ergm.userterms source and unpack it.
     2. Copy the R and C files defining the user-written terms (usually
        changestats.user.h, changestats.user.c, and InitErgmTerm.user.R)
        and *only* those files from the old ergm.userterms source code
        to the new. Do *not* copy the boilerplate files that you did not
        modify.
     3. If you have customized the package DESCRIPTION file (e.g., to
        change the package name) or zzz.R (e.g., to change the startup
        message), modify them as needed, but do *not* simply overwrite
        them with their old versions.
     4. Make sure that your ergm is up to date, and rebuild
        ergm.userterms.

None of this entails changing any aspect of your actual implementation
of the change statistics or of their initialization. You will simply
need to transplant the statistics into the updated boilerplate. Also,
this will only need to be done once, at least for the foreseeable
future: updates to ergm after this upcoming one will not break
ergm.userterms. At worst, you might need to recompile your customized
package without modifying it.*

We (the Statnet Team) would like to know if this transition is likely to
present any difficulties for you. Please let us know.

Lastly, the 3.0-999 preview release does not implement the
aforementioned mechanism to keep things in sync, so do not make the
changes yet.

                        Pavel Krivitsky (on behalf of the Statnet Team)

* --- If we add new features to the package in the future, you may need
to repeat this updating process in order to make use of them. However,
the existing features should continue working even without that.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Checking degeneracy and GOF for multiple networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Checking degeneracy and GOF for multiple networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,

There are two issues I need some help with and I hope somebody can give me advice on them. I tried to keep it short, but I kind of failed? sorry for that!

I want to estimate ergms for a couple of hundred high school class networks (friendship).

I aimed to automate the process and flag classes in which a specified ergm leads to degeneracy or doesn't fit well. I know that usually, one would inspect the mcmc diagnostics plots and the goodness of fit using the gof command, but this would be too labour intensive for the amount of networks I want to estimate.
Up till now, I've thought of storing the log likelihood and the change in the log likelihood between the 2nd and 3rd generation as an indication of degeneracy: both should be small (let's say, not larger than 5).
For the model fit, I planned to store the p-values that the gof command provides (distance, edgewise shared partners, dyadwise shared partners, indegree, outdegree and triad census) as an indication that the simulated networks come from the same distribution as the observed network.
My current decision rule is that I consider a model not to fit a network well if the mean p-value of either one of the structural features is below 0.80 (as high school classes are relatively small and I think that the hypothesis being tested in these tests is the opposite, that is, do the simulated networks significantly differ from the observed network, right?).
When the model doesn't fit according to these criteria, I planned to estimate a different model by adding or removing certain parameters until I get the model to fit all networks.

My question is: does this make sense? Or is there a better strategy?

A second question concerns the actual result of my current strategy: in the majority of the networks, my current model leads to high values of the log likelihood and change in the loglikelihood (indicates degeneracy), and a bad fit according to the gof indicators.

My question: I tried a few things to get rid of degeneracy, such as using gwesp, gwdsp, gwidegree gwodegree (and decrease alpha step by step as well, or keeping them fixed of not fixed); increasing burn in and sample size,  add more attributes, add different terms as cycle(k) and transitive, but nothing I did so far seemed to work sufficiently. Also, there are so many options that might even need to be combined: I would love to get some advice on how I can tackle this problem efficiently.


Best wishes and many thanks in advance,

Sanne Smith
Phd student Utrecht University


ps.

The initial, basic model I tried to fit is:

model1 <-ergm (net ~ edges +
                mutual +
                gwesp(0.2, fixed = TRUE) +
                gwidegree(0.2, fixed = TRUE) +
                gwodegree(0.2, fixed = TRUE) +
                gwdsp(0.2, fixed = TRUE) +
                nodematch("ethnicity") +
                nodematch("gender") +
                absdiff("popular") +
                absdiff("math proficiency") +
                absdiff("language proficiency") +
                absdiff("opinion about social issues (e.g., abortion") +                nodematch("smoke") +
                absdiff("going out") +
                nodecov("ethnicity") +
                nodecov("gender") +
                nodecov("popular") +
                nodecov("math proficiency") +
                nodecov("language proficienc") +
                nodecov("opinion") +
                nodecov("smoke") +
                nodecov("going out")
                , burnin= 50000,MCMCsamplesize= 100000, verbose=TRUE)

and the nr, of actors in the networks ranges from 10 to 30. Also, there is enough variation on the attributes (e.g, at least three immigrants  and three majority members).
